title: VC0-01523
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: The Appellant, XXXX XXXX, is a citizen of Nigeria who has appealed a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) rejecting his claim for refugee protection. For the reasons set out below, the appeal is denied.

Mr. XXXX alleges that he fears persecution in Nigeria, as a gay man. He states that he struggled with his sexuality from the time that he was a child, and that his first same-sex relationship occurred at this time, with a fellow XXXX XXXX in his church. He notes that when this long-term relationship was discovered by church officials, he was expelled from seminary school. He would later go on to study abroad in Malaysia, where he obtained his bachelor's and master's degrees and had a long term same-sex relationship, before he returned to Nigeria and married his wife. He states that in XXXX 2017 his wife's cousin and two other men caught him with a male partner and shamed them publicly, leading to his arrest and detention by the police.

The Appellant alleges that when he was released from custody days later, he immediately left his hometown and went to Lagos to stay with a close family member. He states he then filed for divorce, and that his wife, who was devastated by this, urged him to come home, threatening him with exposure. In XXXX 2018 the police came to his family member's house in Lagos, and he later fled to Canada, arriving on XXXX XXXX, 2018, where he made a claim for refugee protection.

The RPD rejected the claim and concluded that the Appellant and his allegations lacked credibility. It specifically found that: a. While the Appellant's testimony largely echoed the general claims made in his Basis of Claim (BOC) narrative, he was repeatedly unable to flesh out these allegations with specific details or provide personal context to expand on or clarify what he had seen, experienced, or meant, when questioned. He was unable to explain or describe, with specificity, his lifelong struggle with his sexuality when asked, or provide meaningful details about the relationship he was in when he lived in Malaysia, all of which significantly undermined his overall credibility; b. The Appellant gave contradictory and/or evolving testimony with respect to his allegations respecting: his childhood same-sex relationship, his attendance at a gay nightclub once he was in Canada, his stay with a close family member in Lagos, and the divorce from his wife, which all also significantly undermined his credibility; c. The witness testimony of the Appellant's sister was not reliable and the RPD assigned it little weight in supporting his allegations; and d. Ultimately that, due to his lack of credibility, the Appellant failed to establish that that he was a sexual minority, as alleged, and accordingly that he was not a Convention refugee or person in need of protection.

The Appellant has appealed the RPD decision and is now asking the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) to recognize him as a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection, or, in the alternative, to refer this matter back to the RPD for redetermination. He has not requested an oral hearing, nor is he seeking to submit new evidence in the context of this appeal.1 He essentially argues that the RPD's findings of his lack of credibility were not the result of proper reasoned analysis, but rather that the RPD "cherry picked"2 the Appellant's answers in coming to its conclusion and that, further, the conduct of the RPD Member in the hearing raises a reasonable apprehension of bias. He further argues that the RPD erred in its assessment of his credibility, in particular that: a. The RPD failed to properly consider the impact that the Appellant's speech impediment and cognitive difficulties had on his ability to testify, and that this accounted for his failure to provide detail in answering questions; b. Despite the vagueness of some of the RPD's questioning, the responses of the Appellant were sufficiently detailed to explain and provide context and information with respect to his struggle with his sexuality and his relationship in Malaysia; c. Understood in context, the Appellant's testimony was not contradictory with respect to his attendance at a gay nightclub in Calgary, the same-sex relationship of his youth, his time in Lagos and the circumstances of his divorce; and d. The RPD engaged in a microscopic examination of the evidence, and even if there was some basis for making negative credibility determinations, it was not sufficient to support a finding impugning the Appellant's credibility.

The RAD dismisses the appeal and confirms the decision of the RPD that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee, nor a person in need of protection, pursuant to paragraph 111(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act3 (IRPA).

The Refugee Appeal Division reviews decisions of the RPD on a standard of correctness after conducting an independent assessment of the evidence before it.4 The exception to this rule is that the RAD may apply a deferential standard in certain circumstances.5 I have conducted my own independent assessment of all of the evidence in this case, including the oral recording and transcript of the RPD hearing. I find the appropriate standard in this case is one of correctness. In deciding this appeal, I have carefully taken into account the Immigration and Refugee Board's Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity and Expression (SOGIE) Guideline.6 ANALYSIS Summary

The RPD found that the Appellant was not credible, due to a series of inconsistencies in his testimony that he could not reasonably explain, and his inability to provide meaningful detail in relation to his allegations. As noted below, while I disagree that all of the supposed inconsistencies should be held to impugn the credibility of the Appellant, on the whole a review of the evidence indicates that the RPD did not err in concluding the Appellant generally lacked credibility and I agree with the RPD's findings. This includes their finding that he did not establish, on a balance of probabilities, that he is a sexual minority and thus that there is a serious possibility of persecution if he were to return to Nigeria. I further find, based on the evidence before me, that there is not a reasonable apprehension of bias in relation to the conduct of the RPD in the hearing. The conduct of the RPD does not raise a reasonable apprehension of bias

The Appellant essentially submits that he was subjected to a breach of procedural fairness because of the RPD's behaviour during the hearing, and at paragraph 25 of his memorandum correctly sets out the governing legal framework with respect to assessing reasonable apprehension of bias. The Appellant claims that the RPD's behaviour was "antagonistic" at the beginning of the hearing, and that during closing submissions, the RPD "interrupted counsel numerous times inhibiting the ability of counsel to respond to the Panel's concerns raised during the hearing."7 Having reviewed the evidence in this matter, including the audio recording of the RPD hearing, and considered the governing legal framework8 I do not agree that the conduct of the RPD raised a reasonable apprehension of bias, or occasioned a breach of natural justice.
Indeed, there are a number of difficulties with this argument.

First, I note the Appellant does not actually identify any specific examples of the supposedly antagonistic behaviour at the outset of the RPD hearing. Beyond this, having reviewed the hearing audio recording, I do not share the Appellant's characterization of the RPD's conduct. Though the RPD did disallow certain of the Appellant's late applications to introduce evidence at the outset of the hearing (among them, the last moment disclosure of a series of different documents and an attempt to add a witness) and explained to counsel that these requests were being made late and should have been submitted in the normal course, this exchange was in no way antagonistic or somehow marked by hostility. Indeed, listening to the hearing audio recording, the RPD's tone was instead mostly pleasant, and where the Panel interrupted counsel, it was for the purpose of preventing counsel from moving on to another issue before they had finished with the one at hand. I also note that RPD ultimately decided to allow the testimony of the new witness and admitted a number of the documents.

Second, while it is not clear if the Appellant, in this submission, is claiming that the RPD behaved in an antagonistic fashion toward the Appellant himself, as opposed to his counsel, at the outset of the hearing, I do not find this to be case either. In fact, the Panel interacted with the Appellant in a pleasant and straightforward way, and clearly attempted to put the Appellant at ease through both her informal manner and by carefully explaining the process of the hearing, so as to make it less intimidating. When, later in testimony, the RPD noted inconsistencies or the Appellant's failure to answer its questions, this was also done in a non-confrontational manner, with the Panel explaining exactly what the problem with the testimony was, and inviting the Appellant to explain or clarify it. The RPD's questions were aimed at assisting the Appellant in understanding the issues and what was required of him. I also note that when the Appellant seemed to struggle, the RPD would give him time to think and compose himself. In fact, it seemed that a strong rapport was developed between the RPD and the Appellant, to the point where the Appellant was at ease enough to chuckle along with the RPD Member when she chided herself for making a gaffe, early on.

Third, with respect to the RPD's alleged interruptions of Appellant's counsel during his closing submissions, in his appeal the Appellant identifies only one such occurrence. He states that the RPD warned counsel not to testify and introduce evidence when counsel was explaining that the word "sister" has a wide-ranging meaning in Nigeria, such that it could refer to close female relatives such as cousins. The Appellant asserted that counsel had merely been repeating what had been said by his witnesses in testimony, not providing new evidence.

Again, I disagree that the behaviour of the RPD was in any way untoward here. From review of the audio recording and transcript of the hearing, it is clear that Appellant's counsel was indeed only repeating what his witnesses had said about what the word "sister" could refer to in Nigeria. However, counsel then went on start discussing the cultural background in Nigeria and how boys who enjoyed being in the kitchen and cooking are regarded. It was only at this point that the RPD intervened to say that it appeared that he had veered into giving evidence, and cautioned him against doing so. This caution was not given regarding the discussion of the word sister, as indicated by the Appellant in his memorandum. Further, in providing new information with respect to the cultural context relating to boys and cooking, it appears to me that counsel was providing fresh information and evidence, and that the RPD was correct to caution him in this regard.

While the Appellant does not provide other examples of the RPD interrupting his counsel's final submissions, I do think it is fair to say that the exchange between the RPD and counsel did become mildly heated at one point. On that occasion, the RPD intervened to correct an instance where the Panelist felt that their view of an issue had been misconstrued and, further, explained that they objected to the negative characterization that they "threw" a question at the claimant.9 Counsel apologized for this, and rephrased the question, but the issue did not escalate - the RPD thanked him for the apology and the closing submissions continued unabated. Regardless, from the audio recording, it is clear that counsel was in no way inhibited from presenting his arguments or otherwise giving fulsome submissions - he had every opportunity to continue with his arguments, and was given ample opportunity by the RPD to do so. Indeed, counsel did in fact do so, and it was he alone who decided when to conclude his submissions. In my view, the exchanges between the RPD and Appellant's counsel were relatively routine, not problematic, and certainly do not rise to the level of triggering a reasonable apprehension of bias under the law.

Finally, it is important to consider that at the RPD hearing, the Appellant's counsel did not raise any issues of natural justice or procedural fairness. There was no objection at any point in the hearing regarding the RPD's conduct. This is significant, as breaches of procedural fairness must be raised at the earliest possible opportunity.10 If the RPD's conduct was as poor as the Appellant now alleges, it is not reasonable that this issue has only arisen on appeal, after the Appellant's claim had already been rejected.

In sum, based on my own assessment of the hearing record, I find that the RPD's conduct did not give rise to a breach of procedural fairness or natural justice. THE RPD'S CREDIBILITY ASSESSMENT The RPD did not fail to consider the impact of the Appellant's speech impediment or cognitive abilities

The Appellant further contends that the RPD's credibility determination was unreasonable, in part because the "Panel underestimated the impact that the Appellant's speech impediment and cognitive ability had on his ability to testify",11 and that he disagreed with the RPD's assessment that "the claimant was clearly able to understand and answer questions."12 In essence, the Appellant indicates that this may account for his failure to provide detail in answering questions.
Again, after an assessment of the hearing record, I disagree. The Appellant's condition was identified as only a speech impediment

First, I note that it is essentially only in his appeal, as opposed to the RPD hearing, that the Appellant now seems to be claiming that he suffers from cognitive deficiencies that may have impacted his ability to testify. In the RPD hearing, while the Appellant raised the issue of accommodation as one of his requests at the outset of the hearing, upon questioning it became clear that at that point he and his counsel had identified the Appellant's condition as only a speech impediment, as opposed to a cognitive issue of any sort.

In particular, after counsel attempts to raise the accommodation request, the transcript of the hearing notes13 that the following exchange ensues: MEMBER: Why am I getting this now and not prior to the proceeding? COUNSEL: It is something that just came up with his ability to testify. MEMBER: How did this just come up? Have you ever spoken to the gentleman before this hearing? COUNSEL: Yes. MEMBER: So why? COUNSEL: He was -- he was confident that his stammering and his condition, he won't be able to testify.

I note that on listening to the audio recording of the hearing, it is clear that counsel actually said the word "would", rather than "won't" in the last line (which appears to have been erroneously transcribed) - which makes sense contextually, as counsel is explaining why he did not raise this issue beforehand, by saying that his client had been confident that even with his stammering he would be able to testify.14

Regardless, both here and later in the exchange, it is clear that it is only the stammering speech impediment that is being discussed, despite that counsel also uses the word "condition" in the noted exchange.15 At no point here does counsel explain that there is anything more than a stammer or mention that other, cognitive issues are at play. Accordingly, the RPD went on to say that stammering or stuttering alone is typically not the kind of condition that falls under the vulnerable person's guidelines,16 and noted that an application to have a claimant designated as a vulnerable person should have been made early in the RPD process, and should be supported by some form of medical evidence, if such a condition had come into play.

However, the RPD nonetheless then goes on to solicit counsel's input on how the stuttering issue should be addressed to ensure the Appellant is able to effectively testify: MEMBER: So what's -- I -- I hear -- what do you want me to do? COUNSEL: It's just to -- to be mindful of his -- his testimony, his condition when he's testifying, that's all. I understand that this is late, and it's really not much you ---17

The RPD then goes on to note that, in reality, counsel is not asking it to do anything here beyond the standard obligation of a good Board member to be patient and understanding and to take steps to ensure the party has the time and opportunity to testify effectively. Counsel does not dispute this and, in fact, then directly agrees that this is the case.

More importantly, the Member then goes on to clarify and address the situation, saying to the Appellant directly: MEMBER: But I'm going to speak to Mr. XXXX about -- so Counsel's suggested I be mindful, okay, about your -- you seem to have a stammer -- speech impediment? CLAIMANT: Yes. Yes. MEMBER: Okay. And does this -- does the stammering get worse with nerves? CLAIMANT: Yeah. MEMBER: Okay, right. Is there anything that helps you alleviate stammering? CLAIMANT: If I -- if I breathe in and breathe out then calm down then if I walk in place. MEMBER: Okay. Perfect. How about if we take breaks every 30 minutes. Would that help? Or not really? Okay. CLAIMANT: Not really. MEMBER: Okay. And how about if you tell me at any point if you need to take a break today? CLAIMANT: Okay. MEMBER: Okay? That'll help that also I'll let you know that I -- we'll only probably talk for an hour at a time. CLAIMANT: Okay. MEMBER: So once we start asking questions, usually monitor and then we'll stop. Okay? How about --- so nerves will affect it. CLAIMANT: Yeah. MEMBER: And then okay. Any other things that affect it or impact? CLAIMANT: No, those are --- MEMBER: No? Okay. All right. So for you, I ask that you just breathe as much as possible. CLAIMANT: Okay. MEMBER: Okay? And I'll try my best in monitoring the situation as well, okay? CLAIMANT: All right, all right. MEMBER: To help you with your nerves -- CLAIMANT: Okay.18

In this exchange, the RPD makes clear that its understanding is that the Appellant has a stutter, and this is the "condition" that is being discussed throughout the entire dialogue. Importantly, I note that at no point does either the Appellant or counsel intervene to indicate that the issue is anything more than a stutter or explain that there are any cognitive issues in addition to the stammering. Similarly, at the conclusion of the hearing, the RPD directly says to the Appellant that he did well in his testimony and that it thought that his stuttering did not hinder his testimony or giving responses, and again, neither the Appellant nor his counsel disagreed with this statement or alluded to any cognitive issue.19 Despite this, I note that sometime later, in closing submissions, counsel for the Appellant - for the first time - vaguely alludes to "obvious impediments that hindered him from remembering some events and explaining himself",20 without explaining what these impediments were, much less providing medical support for this claim.

In my view, having never reasonably identified a cognitive, as opposed to stuttering, condition in the RPD proceeding, the Appellant cannot reasonably now claim that it was rather such a condition that had impacted his testimony.
I also note that the Appellant has still not sought to introduce any medical evidence supporting the existence of a cognitive issue, in this appeal. The Appellant displayed no cognitive issues

In any event, contrary to the claims of the Appellant, from my review of the hearing audio recording, I find there is no evidence that the Appellant was cognitively struggling with understanding and responding to the RPD's questions throughout his testimony. Listening to the recording, it becomes clear that the vast majority of the responses of the Appellant to the questions posed to him are essentially instantaneous. There is no lag time in his responding - indicating that, for the most part, the questions were immediately understood.
Indeed, on those rare occasions where the Appellant does not understand a question, he does not hesitate to directly alert the RPD, and to ask for clarification or for the question to be repeated.

While there are certainly instances where the Appellant hesitates and obviously struggles to answer the RPD's questions, in my view this is not because of lack of comprehension, but rather because he is being confronted by contradictions in his testimony that he appears to lack explanations for.

Finally, I note that from the record it is clear that the RPD generally took steps to ensure that the Appellant's stuttering did not impact his testimony. Where the Appellant stammered (and even when he didn't), he was given plenty of time to testify and conclude what he wished to say. He was also given an opportunity to slow down and compose himself, when it was needed. Further, the RPD often explained or rephrased its questions, and would even explain why it was asking certain questions to ensure that the context of what was being asked was clear.

In sum, I see no evidence that the testimony of the Appellant was impacted by his stuttering, or by cognitive issues, and I reject, on a balance of probabilities, that any such condition was responsible for failures to provide adequate detail in his testimony, as has now been claimed by the Appellant. The RPD did not err in finding that the Appellant's inability to provide meaningful detail in relation to his struggle with his sexuality and romantic relationships damaged his credibility The Appellant's struggle with his sexuality

As previously noted, the RPD made a number of findings which established that the Appellant was not credible with regard to his allegations, and credibility was, accordingly, the determinative issue in this appeal.

One overarching finding was essentially that while the Appellant's testimony largely reiterated the general claims made in his BOC narrative, he was repeatedly unable to flesh out these allegations with specific details or provide personal context to expand on or clarify what he had experienced or meant. The RPD noted, for example, that upon questioning, he was unable to detail, explain or describe with specificity what he had referred to in his BOC as his lifelong struggle with his sexuality.

Upon review of the record, I note that the RPD asked, in an open-ended question, that the Appellant tell her about that struggle. The Appellant responded by essentially repeating verbatim what his BOC narrative had recorded about this issue: that he didn't feel right in his body, and he didn't do what straight boys do. When the RPD then asked him to describe what he meant by that, he then repeated the next sentence in the BOC narrative on this topic: that when his friends were playing football, he was at home in the kitchen with his mother or doing things that girls preferred doing.21 When the RPD asked what he meant by activities that girls preferred, taking him beyond the detail in the BOC, he cited reading novels, painting nails or watching movies - and when asked how these activities were gender specific, the Appellant stated "that is what gay people do, not straight boys".22

This led to a further exchange where the RPD asks the Appellant what it is that gay people do and is told that they paint their nails and "rub lipstick". The RPD then again asks "So what was your struggle", returning to the central question that the Appellant had failed to answer. When the Appellant did not respond, the RPD continued to give the Appellant the opportunity to explain what he meant, by asking "when you say your sexual identity is gay, what does that mean?." The Appellant responded by reiterating the BOC passage that it meant doing things that girls like to do, not what straight boys ought to do, but again providing no detail as to what those things were. The RPD would then try again to elicit this information, asking directly what kind of things the Appellant did, if he felt more comfortable as a girl. The Appellant did not answer this question, but eventually responded only that "I would love to meet someone who is like me" and, when further prompted, clarifying that this meant gay men.23

In this exchange, I find that the Appellant was unable to explain or describe with any specificity, detail or personal perspective the struggle with his sexuality that is the cornerstone of his refugee claim. After my own independent assessment, I agree with the RPD that it is suspicious that the Appellant was unable to clarify or expand upon the narrative in his BOC, and can understand why the RPD asserted that it appeared that the Appellant was merely reiterating cultural stereotypes about gay people when asked questions, rather than detailing his personal experience or feelings. Like the RPD, I also find that given the Appellant's inability to at all explain his lifelong struggle, the Appellant's testimony in this regard is, on a balance of probabilities, likely not genuine and that his credibility is significantly undermined.

I note that in relation to this issue, in his appeal the Appellant argues that he did adequately define his struggle, citing disparate facts such as that he had to keep his relationship a secret, that he found it difficult to make friends, that he was pressured to marry and that he lost his position as an XXXX XXXX. These are all examples of allegedly negative events in the Appellant's life which are generally noted at various points throughout the Appellant's BOC narrative and reiterated with little detail in his testimony, however, the Appellant did not mention or describe any of them when directly asked to detail his struggle.

I further note that in the Appellant's memorandum, he states that the RPD failed to take into account the testimony of his sister, which he claims "by implication" corroborated his claim that as a child he preferred doing what girls do.24 In my view, the RPD did not fail to take this claim into account. Rather, as the RPD noted, it gave little weight to the sister's testimony, as she was found to be an unreliable witness who repeatedly stated that she knew little about her brother. I have reached the same conclusion, and adopt the RPD's reasoning at paragraph 23 of its Reasons for Decision, in relation to this point. Incidentally, upon review of the record, I also disagree that the sister's testimony provided any such corroboration, in any event. His sister said only that when they were young the Appellant liked playing with her and her friends and that he had a hard time making his own friends;25 this might well be, but that is a far cry from proving that the Appellant generally preferred doing things that girls did. I also note that nowhere in the Appellant's testimony did he himself actually mention that he spent time with his sister's friends or enjoyed doing what they did. The Appellant's romantic relationships

The Appellant was similarly unable to provide detail or personal perspective in relation to his long-term romantic relationships. With respect to his initial, formative same-sex relationship, he was unable to answer simple questions from the RPD, such as what were his feelings when he discovered he was attracted to a fellow XXXX XXXX N.26 Again, in his response, the Appellant largely repeated the passage from the BOC narrative in this regard - that everyone in the church liked this individual and that he was popular. When the RPD followed up by asking if he had any concerns or reservations when he discovered the attraction to another boy, he unequivocally said that he did not. When the RPD asked why he thought he had not had any such concerns, the Appellant gave confusing testimony saying only that he wanted the two of them to know each other well, before he would have taken him on a date. When the RPD asked whether it was common for children of 12 (the age he was when this supposedly happened) to date, or for boys to date each other, the Appellant conceded it was not, but had no answer for how he then had thought he would date N. (or why he had no concerns about this attraction).

I note that in the Appellant's memorandum, the Appellant objects to the questions the RPD asked with respect to this relationship. He states that "The Panel asked vague questions such as 'what were your feelings when you discovered that you were attracted to N.?' and expected a clear answer," and also asserts that the RPD did not ask a single specific question about N.27 I disagree that any of this was problematic. The RPD did effectively question the Appellant about the relationship, but simply did so in an open-ended way. Generally asking the Appellant to talk about his feelings upon discovering he was attracted to a boy, N., provided an open opportunity for him to speak about his memories, perspective and emotions in relation to this, as he saw fit. That the Appellant was unable to do any of that, but rather only essentially reiterated the script from his BOC narrative, rightfully aroused the RPD's suspicion. Similarly, the RPD asked further open questions about the relationship with N. that gave the Appellant the latitude to discuss what he wanted to in relation to this, yet despite extensive further prompting when nothing of substance was revealed, again he provided no detail or personal perspective of consequence. Indeed, upon my review of the record, it is my view that the RPD's questioning of the Appellant in this regard was not only appropriate, but also accorded with section 7.3 of the SOGIE guidelines, which recommends that questioning should be sensitive and non-confrontational, and which specifically notes that open-ended questioning should be employed where appropriate.

With respect to the Appellant's boyfriend in Malaysia, he was again able to provide almost no detail with respect to this five-year relationship. He responded to extensive questioning by the RPD with only the barest of generalities, such as saying that P. was nice and he wanted to be with him, and that they were close, but providing little detail about the relationship or his personal perspective with relation to it. When specifically asked what they would do together, he said only that he would help P. cook. When the RPD cautioned that it was not being given a sense of the relationship or who P. was, and asked "Can you help me understand who P. is? Paint me the picture of who P. is", the Appellant said only that he was loving.28 As with the childhood relationship in Nigeria, the Appellant was able to give no meaningful detail about this five-year relationship or insight into his feelings about it.

I note that in the Appellant's memorandum, he asserts that the detail he provided with respect to this relationship was sufficient, and argues that the RPD should have been mindful of his cognitive impediments in evaluating it.29 I disagree. As previously noted, I have found that the Appellant's inability to provide such detail in his testimony was not due to cognitive difficulties, as claimed in the appeal. As the RPD did, I find that the testimony given with respect to Appellant's alleged foundational same-sex relationships was not supported with the level of detail or personal perspective that one would reasonably expect in the circumstances. I further find, on a balance of probabilities that the testimony in relation to these events was not genuine and reliable, and that this too undermined the Appellant's credibility. The RPD did not err in finding that the Appellant's contradictory and evolving testimony undermined his credibility

In its analysis, the RPD also found the testimony of the Appellant to be replete with a series of contradictions in relation to his childhood same-sex relationship and his time as an XXXX XXXX, his stay with a close family member in Lagos, and the divorce from his wife, among other things. The RPD noted that when he was questioned about these issues, the Appellant's testimony evolved suspiciously, and found that his credibility was further undermined.
The Appellant, on the other hand, disputes that this testimony was contradictory in his appeal. The Appellant's time as an XXXX XXXX and relationship with N.

Upon my review of the record, I agree with the RAD that the Appellant's testimony in relation to his time with N. as an XXXX XXXX was contradictory and evasive. When questioned, the Appellant changed his testimony multiple times as to the length of his service as an XXXX XXXX. This is particularly notable because this was allegedly the same period of time that he was involved in a relationship with N., whom he had served as an XXXX XXXX with. Originally, in his testimony, the Appellant could not provide an answer when asked by the RPD how long he had been an XXXX XXXX before being caught with N. and summarily removed, though he did note that he had first become an XXXX XXXX at the age of 12. Later, he vaguely testified that he "had not been an XXXX XXXX long" before they were caught. Later still, he stated that it was actually four years. However, in his BOC narrative he stated that they were caught XXXX XXXX XXXX before they were to go to seminary school, and when asked in testimony what age he was supposed to go to seminary school, he testified this would have been when he was 21. That would mean that it would have instead been at least eight or nine years that he and N. had been XXXX XXXX, and in a relationship, before being caught.

The RPD also noted, as do I, that the Appellant's testimony in this regard was also contradicted by that of his sister, who was one of his witnesses. The Appellant testified that he had spent a lifetime being prepared for becoming a priest before being caught, and having this path foreclosed to him. However, despite being close in age with the Appellant, his sister testified that she knew nothing of this, as she had been unaware of any plans he had for the future while growing up. I adopt the reasoning of the RPD with respect to this inconsistency, as I, too, would reasonably expect that had the claimant been groomed to be a priest by the church and his family from childhood to almost the age of 21, surely the family, including his closest sister, would have had some knowledge of it. I find that the Appellant's testimony with relation to his time as an XXXX XXXX and his relationship with N. was internally inconsistent, evolving and contradicted by his sister, which undermines these allegations, including with respect to having had the relationship with N. during this time.

I further note that this finding is significant, as it goes to the very heart of the Appellant's claim. His relationship with N. is central to his narrative, as it was this which allegedly led him to realize that he was gay, and it was being caught with N. by church officials that caused the issues with his family, triggered his seeking to study abroad and led to everything else. That the allegations of serving as an XXXX XXXX and the attendant relationship with N. have been significantly undermined throws into serious doubt not only the existence of N., but the foundation of the Appellant's entire claim. The Appellant's time in Lagos
There were also significant contradictions in the evidence of the Appellant with respect to the time that he stayed with a close relative in Lagos, prior to his departure from Nigeria to Canada.

The RPD found it suspicious that the Appellant described the relative that he stayed with as his sister, when it later emerged that this person was actually his cousin. However, I accept as reasonable the Appellant's explanation that the term sister can be used more loosely in Nigerian culture, and may be applied to range of close female relatives, rather than strictly to one's siblings. I do not find that this inconsistency undermines the credibility of the Appellant.

I cannot say the same, however, with respect to the contradictions that arose in the Appellant's evidence with respect to the time period that the Appellant allegedly stayed with this relative after he went to Lagos. According to his BOC narrative, the Appellant left for Lagos to live with his "sister" shortly after being released from police detention in XXXX 2017, and stayed there until he fled to Canada in XXXX 2018. However, as was raised with the Appellant by the RPD, the letter from his cousin submitted into evidence states that he only spent "a few days" with her.30 When questioned about this contradiction, the Appellant testified that he did not spend that entire time at his cousin's house, but that after the police came looking for him there he had to stay with a friend.

However, even taken at face value, there remains a problem with this explanation. It was consistent in both the Appellant's BOC narrative and his testimony that the police came to his cousin's house looking for him in XXXX 2018, as it was at that time that the Appellant concluded that he needed to flee from Nigeria. This would mean that, even with his explanation, it appears that he still stayed at his cousin's from around XXXX 2017 until XXXX 2018, a far cry from the "few days" cited by his cousin. I also note that when asked to explain why it appeared that his testimony was changing upon being told of the contradictory evidence from his cousin, the Appellant had no response. I further note that upon appeal, while the Appellant took issue with the RPD's finding that he had not been hiding, and argued that he had originally thought his wife's threats were empty in answer to why he did not flee sooner, at no point did he address the discrepancy in the timing or the sequence of when he stayed with his cousin, except to now say that he had "intermittently" stayed with his cousin and a friend. I find that the contradictions in relation to the Appellant's time with his cousin in Lagos significantly undercut his allegations of hiding in Lagos as claimed, and that this also undermines his credibility.

I also note that both the RPD decision and the Appellant's memorandum discuss another apparent contradiction, as to whether the Appellant once attended a gay club in Canada. Again, a review of the record indicates that under questioning by the RPD, the Appellant appears to have provided contradictory testimony in relation to this incident that significantly throws into question whether he actually attended the establishment at all (or alternately if he really did so as a patron as opposed to having just briefly passed by to scope out the location). Regardless, I note that even if it is accepted that the Appellant were to have gone to the establishment, I find, on a balance of probabilities, that this event would likely not have come to the attention of the authorities in Nigeria, and does not reasonably give rise to a sur place risk of persecution in Nigeria. The Appellant's divorce

Finally, I note that with respect to the Appellant's divorce, his BOC narrative states clearly that after he fled to Lagos, he met with a lawyer, filed for divorce and served his wife with divorce papers. The narrative goes on to state that this devastated her, that she begged him to come home to fix the marriage and, when he refused to do so, she threatened to report his sexuality to the police. He goes on to say that this is what happened, as the police later came to his cousin's house looking for him, and that all of this triggered his flight to Canada. However, as was noted by the RPD, the Lagos High Court Dissolution of Marriage document submitted into evidence establishes that it was actually the Appellant's ex-wife who had sought the divorce and that she was, in fact, the sole petitioner in respect of it.31 Upon questioning, the Appellant's testimony varied from the narrative, as he then claimed that his lawyer had recommended that his ex-wife petition for the divorce to speed up the process. However, the Appellant was able to offer no response when the RPD pointed out that the official divorce documents indicated that he had no legal representation in the proceeding and had been absent from the matter entirely.32 Upon questioning by his counsel, the Appellant later could only testify that his Nigerian lawyer had not discussed with him how he would go about securing the divorce.33

I do not find this explanation persuasive. Even if the Appellant did not know how his lawyer had gone about obtaining the divorce, he surely would have known what he himself was writing in his BOC narrative. Given that the divorce and the court documents in relation to it had been issued by XXXX XXXX, 2018, some XXXX months before he left Nigeria for Canada, I find his inclusion of the contrary information in the BOC to be an additional factor that diminishes the credibility of the Appellant's claims with respect to his divorce. I note that this is, again, particularly significant, as it calls into question his claims that his wife set the police on him in Lagos, which was supposedly the catalyst for his deciding to flee to Canada.

In short, I find that the many and serious instances of contradictory and evolving testimony of the Appellant severely, and generally, undermine his credibility. I also find that contrary to the claims of the Appellant, the RPD did not err by engaging in a microscopic analysis and basing its credibility findings on peripheral issues. As I have noted, there are a series of key omissions, discrepancies, and evidentiary contradictions that have resulted in my finding of the Appellant's loss of credibility.

For the foregoing reasons, and based upon my own analysis of the record, I agree with the finding of the RPD that the Appellant is not a credible witness. I further find that, on a balance of probabilities, the Appellant was not credible with regard to his allegations that he had been involved in same-sex relationships in Nigeria or Malaysia, or had been sought by the police while staying with his cousin in Lagos, all of which were events that ultimately led to his flight to Canada and claim of refugee status. These findings go to the core of the Appellant's narrative, and I find that he has not established, on a balance of probabilities, that he is a sexual minority. I therefore concur with the RPD decision that the Appellant's claim is not established, on a balance of probabilities.

Accordingly, the RAD dismisses the appeal and confirms the decision of the RPD that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee, nor a person in need of protection, pursuant to paragraph 111(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act.
